transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Anita Rao (SablePoint Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Platform), Priya Desai (Security), Noah Patel (Product), Mike Harris (Guest)

Auto-generated summary: Redwood Optimize demo focused on prefetch (lookahead) vs session KV caching. Walked through cost model scenarios in the console and discussed pilot bench.

Topics: Prefetch vs sessionization, batch sizing, KV TTL and eviction, Sandbox pilot, security/KMS

---- Transcript (timestamps approximate, ASR imperfect) ----
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy holidays, we'll try to keep this tight. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Diego, our SE. Today we'll run an Optimize playbook: prefetch (lookahead) versus session KV cache for your workload, walk through the cost model in the console, and propose a small pilot.

[00:25] Anita Rao: Nice to meet you all. We're especially interested in saving on tokens for our assistant — it's latency sensitive, spikes around market open, high concurrency.

[00:37] Diego Ruiz: Totally. Quick clarifying question — is your current production routing go to a single model type or multi-tiered (like 7B cheap + 70B for fallback)?

[00:46] Liam O'Connor: We do a hybrid: mostly a distilled 8B variant for day-to-day, but for complex reasoning we send to a larger 32B. Fallbacks are manual right now.

[00:58] Diego Ruiz: Got it. That's helpful because prefetch tends to pay off differently depending on model fan-out. We'll show a few scenarios: pure-prefetch, session-only, and a hybrid where prefix hits prime a larger model's KV cache.

[01:12] Anita Rao: Quick note — our latency SLO is 180ms p95 for front-office queries, but some back-office analytics can be relaxed.

[01:20] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll keep that in the tradeoff matrix. Okay, I'll share my screen and open the Optimize console. (screen share noise)

[01:46] Diego Ruiz: Opening the cost model tab. The Console has a scenario builder — you can set request distribution, concurrency, average prompt length, and then toggle caching policies. For SablePoint, we put a sample: 20% long-form (200–400 tokens), 60% short (20–80), 20% follow-ups.

[02:10] Noah Patel: That distribution sounds right. Our follow-ups often reuse the same instrument context, so prefix caching could be high value.

[02:22] Diego Ruiz: Exactly — follow-ups are the low-hanging fruit. First scenario: session KV cache with per-session TTL of 30 minutes and a moderate hit rate assumption of 40%. On the right you can see predicted token savings and cost per 1000 requests.

[02:40] Anita Rao: Is that 40% conservative? In early tests we saw 55% but that included client-side dedup.

[02:48] Diego Ruiz: We intentionally used conservative hit rates; Optimize also lets you import historical traces to estimate hit curves. We'll demo that shortly. The console predicts ~23% token cost reduction for this session strategy at your baseline concurrency.

[03:05] Maya Chen: Second scenario: prefetch / lookahead of the next-turn prefixes. This pushes more prefixes into the KV cache proactively so subsequent calls are shorter. Prefetch increases write bandwidth and slightly increases initial latency on the triggering call, but dramatically reduces downstream token cost if hit rates are high.

[03:28] Liam O'Connor: Our concern there is write IOPS during open — market open is a spike. Would prefetch amplify tail latency?

[03:36] Diego Ruiz: Good question. In our runtime, prefetch is implemented as asynchronous lookahead and can be configured to run on a lower priority queue or offloaded to a dedicated cache priming pool. That means the caller doesn't always wait synchronously for the write. The tradeoff is more burst capacity for prefetching.

[03:56] Priya Desai: From security side, any prefetching that persists user PII into cache needs controls — TTL, encryption, and audit logs. We use customer-managed KMS so we need details on KMS integration.

[04:07] Maya Chen: We'll share our KMS/HSM integration doc. The cache is encrypted at rest and keys can be integrated with your KMS. Also we show audit trails in the Console export.

[04:18] Diego Ruiz: Back to economics — for the same request distribution, prefetch showed a 32–38% token reduction in our sim when hit rate of prefetched prefixes was 60–70%. But if hit rate drops below ~30% prefetch can cost more because of extra priming tokens.

[04:40] Anita Rao: So looks like hybrid might be safest: session caching for all sessions, and selective prefetch for workflows we can predict.

[04:49] Diego Ruiz: Right — we usually recommend an operational plan: start with session KV caching (easy wins), measure effective hit rate post-deploy, and then enable lookahead selectively on high-confidence flows (e.g., instrument lookup + follow-ups).

[05:05] Maya Chen: I'll flip to the scenario matrix — here's a heatmap of latency vs cost for three strategies across concurrency curves. Note the cost slope flattens with batching.

[05:20] Noah Patel: Can you explain how batching interacts with session cache? Our app often aggregates 6-8 short requests into micro-batches on the client.

[05:29] Diego Ruiz: Sure. Continuous batching at the runtime level groups in-flight requests; session cache helps reduce token count per request so the net effect is multiplicative: fewer tokens per request and better packing efficiency. But beware: very large batches can increase individual tail latency — we model p95/p99 separately.

[05:50] Liam O'Connor: What about model variants — if we warm a KV cache for the 8B, but then route to 32B for a fallback, do you keep caches in sync?

[05:58] Diego Ruiz: We support cache routing policies. You can either maintain separate caches per model or set up cache compatibility mapping. For heavy fallbacks you might prime the larger model's cache with prefixes from the smaller model when semantics line up. That increases priming cost but reduces cold-start hits on fallback.

[06:20] Anita Rao: Could that double-count tokens in the cost model? We want to avoid underestimating costs if we prime multiple models.

[06:28] Diego Ruiz: Great point. In the Console we allow you to model multi-model priming overhead explicitly — there's a checkbox to include cross-model priming tokens. We also surfaced a line item in the breakdown: priming writes, read hits, net tokens served, and expected latency delta.

[06:50] Maya Chen: Switching to the trace import — Diego, do the import. We asked Anita earlier for a 48-hour anonymized request trace. If you upload it, Optimize fits an empirical hit curve.

[07:05] Diego Ruiz: (upload sound) Uploaded. The parser found session IDs, average prompt length 68 tokens, median concurrency 120 during spikes. The inferred likely prefix reuse shows a potential 47% hit ceiling for session caching, and 62% for targeted lookahead with top-3 candidate prefixes.

[07:31] Anita Rao: That aligns with our internal estimate. Nice that it infers sessionization. How deterministic is the inference?

[07:38] Diego Ruiz: It's heuristic — uses repeat n-gram overlap and session IDs. We always recommend validating with a quick pilot to measure real-world hit rates.

[07:46] Maya Chen: Now the cost spreadsheet export — you'll see per-strategy sheets: baseline, session-only, prefetch, and hybrid, with per-token cost, priming overhead, and burst capacity needs. I'll scroll to the hybrid sheet.

[08:02] (paper rustle)

[08:08] Diego Ruiz: Hybrid shows a projected 29% cost reduction vs baseline with p95 latency within 150ms under normal load; during spikes with limited burst config it edges to 205ms p95 unless you provision burst capacity or enable automatic fallbacks to a cheaper model for tail traffic.

[08:28] Liam O'Connor: For SLAs we need a guaranteed p95 under heavy open-market loads. Is that a Dedicated capacity conversation?

[08:36] Maya Chen: Yes — Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and burst headroom. You can also mix: run hosted for normal ops and a Dedicated pool for peak windows to hit your SLA without huge overprovisioning.

[08:50] Priya Desai: On compliance, we need to ensure logs are retained for 13 months and that KMS key rotation won't break cache decrypts. Is that supported?

[08:59] Diego Ruiz: Rotation is supported with a grace period; we can outline procedures in the SOC2/ISO docs we share. Logs are exportable to your SIEM and retention windows are configurable on Private deployments — for Hosted there are retention limits you can extend under an enterprise agreement.

[09:20] Noah Patel: About the sandbox pilot — what's the data flow? We prefer to replay traces rather than real production traffic.

[09:28] Diego Ruiz: Absolutely. The recommended pilot is: 3-day replay of anonymized traces into a sandbox cluster provisioned with your model variants, simulate peak concurrency, collect hit rates, tail latencies, and a cost delta. We'll send a template for trace formatting.

[09:45] Anita Rao: Sounds reasonable. How long until we see results?

[09:49] Maya Chen: Once we get the trace, Diego can run the replay and return a 1–2 day summary with console exports.

[09:55] (short pause, background)

[10:10] Diego Ruiz: A practical note on TTL and eviction: for session caches we typically start with 30–60 minutes TTL and LRU eviction; for markets with very high uniqueness (lots of ad-hoc prompts) you could go shorter. TTL interacts strongly with cost — longer TTL increases hit rate but increases memory. The Console shows memory footprint estimates given TTL and expected cardinality.

[10:36] Liam O'Connor: Do you provide cardinality estimators or bloom filters to help keep memory low?

[10:42] Diego Ruiz: We expose approximate counting sketches and an estimated unique session projection in the Optimize export. Also support approximate dedup and fingerprinting strategies to reduce cache pressure.

[10:55] Priya Desai: For encryption, is cache content tokenized or raw prompt stored? We want personal data stripped before caching.
transcript_continued:
[11:05] Maya Chen: You should definitely strip PII — best practice is to run a pre-caching sanitizer. Redwood supports a plugin hook to do that before caching; we can add rules in the sandbox run.

[11:18] Anita Rao: Could you show the priority queue options for prefetch?

[11:22] Diego Ruiz: Sure — under runtime config you can choose synchronous prefetch, async low-priority, or async offloaded pool. In the demo the offloaded pool shows negligible p95 impact on the initiating call but requires capacity headroom during spikes.

[11:40] Maya Chen: Jumping quickly to failure modes: if cache storage is exhausted we fall back to live generation; we also have graceful fallbacks to a cheaper model variant to preserve latency SLOs.

[11:52] Noah Patel: Any guidance on cost thresholds to trigger automatic fallback?

[11:57] Diego Ruiz: We recommend rule-based thresholds: e.g., if write IOPS or memory usage > 80% of provisioned, start probabilistic prefetch throttling; or route new sessions to a cheaper model for a rolling window. The Console can simulate those policies.

[12:15] Anita Rao: Can we run a 50/50 A/B comparing hybrid strategy vs session-only in our traffic?

[12:21] Diego Ruiz: Yes — we support canary rollouts and traffic splitting. For pilot maturity, we usually do a canary to 20% of traffic for a day, measure hit rate and latency, then ramp. We'll add that as a pilot step.

[12:34] Maya Chen: Recap: import traces, run 3-day sandbox replay, get console export, then do small canary in prod or a mirrored stream. We'll capture security requirements and agreement for KMS.

[12:46] Priya Desai: We'll need contract language around data retention and key management. Please send sample amendment.

[12:52] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll include a sample SLA amendment and SOC2 package in the packet.

[13:01] (longer pause — mid-call Q&A continues, summarizing a few smaller clarifications)

[42:12] Diego Ruiz: (mid-call) Quick deep dive on the modeling math — the Console's hit model is basically H = 1 - exp(-alpha * reuse_rate * ttl), where alpha is observed stickiness, reuse_rate is estimated from your trace. It's approximate, but it's transparent so you can tune parameters.

[42:35] Anita Rao: Interesting, we like transparent equations. Could we get the model parameters exported?

[42:40] Diego Ruiz: Yes — the export includes the inferred alpha and TTL curve samples.

[43:05] Noah Patel: One thing — we use strict audit logging to an internal SIEM. Will sandbox logs be isolated?

[43:12] Diego Ruiz: Sandbox logs can be pulled via S3 or a secure endpoint; we'll give you access tokens. We recommend not shipping raw prompts — use anonymized replays.

[44:00] Maya Chen: Alright, we're approaching the last 10 minutes. Final objections/concerns?

[44:12] Priya Desai: KMS integration, retention windows, and auditability are our immediate blockers. Also a legal on cross-model priming token accounting.

[44:22] Maya Chen: We'll put those in the packet. Any other technical asks?

[44:30] Liam O'Connor: Could we get an estimate of Dedicated sizing if we wanted guaranteed p95 at market open?

[44:36] Diego Ruiz: Yes — for your peak concurrency numbers from the trace, the Console's capacity planner suggests starting with a 4-GPU Dedicated pool with autoscale headroom; we'll include the sizing worksheet in the workbook.

[44:50] Anita Rao: Great.

[44:54] Maya Chen: Next steps recap — I'll send the cost workbook and SOC2/KMS docs; Diego will provision the sandbox; Anita will share traces; Priya will enumerate security constraints. We aim to have the pilot kickoff around Jan 11th.

[45:10] Noah Patel: That timeline works for us.

[45:18] Maya Chen: Any final quick Qs?

[45:24] (brief chatter)

[45:40] Maya Chen: Okay thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the packet and calendar invite. Happy holidays.

[46:00] (meeting wrap noise)

End of transcript.
